candidate_datasets.name: GBIF

Natural group and instinctive recognition lack unique measurable criteria.
rationale: Phylogenetic and trait data could compare algorithms, but could not settle the stated prescription without choosing a definition of naturalness in advance. Almost any result can be accommodated by changing the selected differentiae or similarity criterion.

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape Knowledgebase

operationalization: Use lesion, recording, and anatomical evidence to locate neural control of sensation, voluntary movement, and nutrition across vertebrates and representative invertebrates. Central control outside the heart, or distributed among different structures, refutes the claim.

operationalization: Measure blood viscosity, temperature, optical clarity, strength, sensory performance, cognition, and defensive behavior across species under phylogenetic control. The predicted signed associations would support the claim and null or reversed associations would refute it.
obstacles: Courage and intelligence require contested cross-species measures.
Blood properties and behavioral outcomes are not available together at broad taxonomic scale.

operationalization: Compare temperature and phase or viscosity before and after freshly collected blood and yellow bile are removed from the body under standardized conditions. Failure of blood to clot or failure of bile to become less viscous in a taxon refutes the universal wording.
obstacles: Comparable ex vivo time-series data are scattered across clinical and veterinary studies.

rationale: The physical changes and decision criteria are direct. Existing public literature can resolve common mammals, but no broad standardized dataset supports the scope of all blooded animals.

operationalization: Map stomach-sac to a defined digestive chamber and code its presence across a taxonomically representative sample, stratified by locomotion. Numerous mobile animals lacking such a chamber would refute the conspicuous universality.

operationalization: In public fasting and feeding studies, compare blood or hemolymph volume, cell production, nutrient content, and health markers before and after controlled intake. Final nutriment does not map to one modern variable.
Invertebrate hemolymph is not straightforwardly comparable.

Threat protocols and response measures differ radically among clades.
Existing behavioral datasets do not sample both groups comparably.

All other animals is impractically broad.
rationale: The variables are direct, but the global fastest claim demands standardized comparative observations that public veterinary studies do not provide. New harmonized sampling would be needed for an adequate test.

operationalization: Code horn state, upper-incisor state, foot form, and adipose melting and solidification properties for ruminants, pigs, and counterexample taxa. A horned upper-incisor-bearing species or mismatched fat chemistry refutes the categorical association.

operationalization: Compare in vivo brain temperature with core and organ temperatures and quantify brain parenchymal vascularization histologically across animals. Brain temperatures not being the minimum or blood vessels within proper brain substance refute the respective components.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: crocodilian anatomy and feeding behavior accounts

obstacles: Both jaws can change position relative to the environment through head movement, so skull-relative motion is essential.
rationale: The anatomical and kinematic alternatives are precise and public specimens and behavior records are ample. Standard inspection can resolve both tongue attachment and which jaw articulates.

operationalization: Identify purpurae as muricid gastropods and document radular drilling behavior, borehole morphology, and prey shells in observations or experiments. Absence of radular boring or use of a different organ would refute the anatomical mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: authoritative taxonomy for mapping purple-dye snails and prey molluscs

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: gastropod feeding anatomy and behavior accounts

obstacles: Muricids can combine radular rasping with chemical shell dissolution.
Historical purpurae may map to several muricid species.
rationale: Shell drilling by a defined feeding apparatus leaves observable traces and is documented for muricids. Public taxonomy and zoological records can resolve the core behavior, with some ambiguity about the exact ancient species and mechanism.

operationalization: Define tusks as enlarged projecting teeth and saw-like teeth by crown and occlusion morphology, then code their co-occurrence across mammals. A species expressing both states in one individual refutes the categorical exclusion.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: comparative mammal skull and dentition imaging

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: mammalian dentition and feeding accounts

obstacles: Sharp interfitting or saw-like is not a standard dental character.
Tusks themselves are teeth and vary by sex and age.
Functional striking versus biting is not consistently recorded.
rationale: The co-occurrence claim can be screened from skulls and yields decisive counterexamples. Character definitions and incomplete taxonomic coding prevent immediate resolution over all mammals.

operationalization: For specified weapons, quantify morphology and observed use effectiveness across species and sexes, testing whether better users have more developed weapons. The assertion that nature allots them for use has no independent criterion beyond the association.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: comparative morphology of horns, tusks, stings, and spurs

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: behavioral accounts of weapon use

obstacles: Can use and use best require weapon-specific performance metrics.
The final-cause statement is not distinct from observed adaptation.
Weapons have multiple functions.
rationale: Trait-performance associations are empirically accessible for selected weapon systems. They only test a proxy and cannot resolve the universal teleological allocation itself.

operationalization: Measure presence and size of horns, tusks, and spurs by sex within deer, bovids, suids, and spurred birds. Female-only weapons or no male-biased development in covered species refute the sex-pattern component.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: sexed specimen morphology for cranial and limb weapons

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: sexual dimorphism and weapon-use accounts

obstacles: Sex metadata are incomplete for museum specimens.
Female weapons occur in some taxa and ecological contexts.
Strength and spiritedness are not needed to test the morphology but complicate causation.
rationale: Sexual presence and size dimorphism are standard measurable traits with public comparative evidence. Coverage is adequate for named examples but not every weapon-bearing lineage or the causal behavioral explanation.

operationalization: Define serrated or saw-like tooth form and code dentition across major fish lineages, including Mediterranean Sparisoma cretense. Any other fish lacking the form or Scarus possessing it refutes the single-exception claim.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: broad fish taxonomy, feeding, and morphology records

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: fish jaw and tooth imaging

obstacles: Serrated form may refer to teeth arranged like a saw rather than serrations on each tooth.
Fish dentitions are exceptionally diverse and incompletely coded.
Some fishes lack oral teeth.
rationale: The universal and unique-exception claims can be decisively challenged with comparative dentition records. Public resources cover many lineages but require substantial manual coding and cannot guarantee exhaustive fish coverage.

operationalization: For Accipitriformes, Falconiformes, and Strigiformes, code talon curvature, beak shape, and plant matter in diet from morphology and feeding records. Any included species with a nonhooked beak or regular vegetable food refutes the categorical statement.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: raptor morphology and diet accounts

candidate_datasets.name: Macaulay Library
candidate_datasets.role: public images and videos documenting beaks, talons, and feeding

obstacles: Incidental versus nutritionally meaningful plant consumption needs a threshold.
Bird of prey boundaries vary among taxonomies.
rationale: Beak and talon form are conspicuous, and diets of raptors are extensively documented in public sources. The strict no-vegetable-food clause can be resolved through existing records without new observations.

operationalization: Define true horn by tissue composition and developmental homology, then code horn-like structures, reproductive mode, and fighting use across animals. A homologous true horn in an oviparous animal refutes exclusivity.

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: cross-species anatomical definitions and homology relations

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: comparative imaging of cranial projections

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: reproduction and weapon-use accounts

obstacles: True horn is definition-dependent and may make the result partly tautological.
Viviparity has evolved outside mammals.
Fighting use is behaviorally underreported.
rationale: Anatomy and reproductive mode are available, but the true-versus-metaphorical distinction must be fixed independently. Existing data can test modern homologous structures, while the broad wording remains partly conceptual.

operationalization: Compare internal structure and periodic shedding of cervid antlers with permanent bovid horn cores and other cranial appendages. A noncervid with a solid homologous horn that is normally shed, or a cervid appendage not solid, refutes a component.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT and surface anatomy of antlers and other mammalian cranial appendages

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: life-history accounts of antler and horn shedding

obstacles: Aristotle's horn merges antlers and true horns, which modern anatomy separates.
Pronghorn sheath shedding creates a definitional counterexample.
rationale: Internal structure and shedding are well-documented comparative traits. Existing public anatomy and natural-history data can resolve the statement once the historical horn category is explicitly mapped.

operationalization: Code cranial appendage type and upper incisor presence across horned mammals, separating antlers, keratin horns, ossicones, and pronghorns. Any included horned species with upper incisors refutes the anatomical universal; developmental resource diversion requires separate evidence.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: mammal skull imaging showing horns and dentition

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: dentition and cranial-appendage accounts

obstacles: Horn is heterogeneous under modern homology.
Rare developmental anomalies should be separated from species-typical anatomy.
Material subtraction from teeth is not directly observed by co-occurrence.
rationale: The co-occurrence pattern is straightforward to screen across well-sampled mammals. Existing data do not by themselves test the proposed developmental tradeoff, so the full causal claim is only partial.

operationalization: Define neck as a distinct mobile region between head and trunk and code it with lung presence across blooded animals, especially fishes. A lungless animal with such a neck or a lunged animal without one refutes the biconditional implication.

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape Knowledgebase
candidate_datasets.role: vertebrate anatomical phenotype data

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fish respiratory and body-form information

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: comparative vertebrate axial and respiratory anatomy

obstacles: Neck boundaries are difficult in fishes and elongate vertebrates.
Some fishes possess lungs or lung homologues.
The windpipe-purpose explanation is not established by correlation.
rationale: The trait association is observable and vertebrate anatomy is well represented. Definitional and homology issues plus exceptions require specialist coding, and the functional reason is less discriminating.

operationalization: Code an anatomically homologous epiglottis, lungs, and integument across mammals, birds, and reptiles. An epiglottis in a feathered or scaled animal, or its absence in a hairy lunged mammal, refutes exclusivity.

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: cross-species definitions and taxonomic constraints for laryngeal structures

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: comparative head and airway anatomy

obstacles: Epiglottis-like folds may be analogous rather than homologous.
Soft-tissue laryngeal anatomy is underrepresented in museum imaging.
Species-level exceptions are hard to screen exhaustively.
rationale: The co-occurring anatomical traits are measurable and public comparative sources cover major clades. Soft-tissue and homology coverage are insufficient for the universal scope.

operationalization: Define each listed viscus by structure and function, then code homologous or analogous internal organs across vertebrates and major invertebrate phyla. A bloodless animal with an organ meeting the fixed definition refutes the categorical absence.

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: cross-species organ ontology and anatomical homology

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: comparative internal anatomy across animal phyla

obstacles: Viscera may be defined to include only vertebrate homologues, making the claim partly terminological.
Invertebrate organs often perform analogous functions under different names.
rationale: Organ presence is empirical, but category choice determines whether invertebrate hearts, kidneys, or digestive glands count. Existing resources can resolve fixed definitions for major groups, not eliminate the conceptual ambiguity.

operationalization: Use staged embryo imaging and expression data to record first appearance of cardiac tissue, beating, blood cells, and other organs across vertebrates. Any other differentiated part appearing earlier, or cardiac tissue preceding blood content, refutes a component under a fixed stage criterion.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish developmental anatomy, staging, expression, and imaging

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
candidate_datasets.role: frog embryology and developmental anatomy

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus
candidate_datasets.role: public vertebrate embryonic time-course data

obstacles: First formed depends on whether primordium, differentiation, morphology, or function is used.
Open data emphasize a few model vertebrates.
Blood islands may develop outside the heart.
rationale: Developmental order is measurable and model-organism datasets are rich enough for decisive tests in several vertebrates. They do not adequately sample all animals with blood, and the endpoint needs explicit staging.

operationalization: Compare sensory-evoked activity and causal lesion or stimulation effects in brain, peripheral nerves, and heart. Sensation-specific neural activity and loss of sensation after neural disruption despite an intact heart refute the heart-as-primary-seat mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: OpenNeuro
candidate_datasets.role: public sensory-task neuroimaging and electrophysiology

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Brain Map
candidate_datasets.role: public neural circuits, activity, and connectivity resources

candidate_datasets.name: PhysioNet
candidate_datasets.role: paired physiological recordings useful for separating cardiac responses from sensory processing

obstacles: Cardiac responses accompany emotion and pain but do not establish sensory origin.
Cross-phyla causal data are concentrated in models.
rationale: The heart and nervous-system accounts make sharply discriminating causal predictions. Existing public human and animal neuroscience data are sufficient to resolve the central assertion without collecting new data.

operationalization: Measure heart centroid relative to the sagittal plane in humans and a broad vertebrate sample from imaging. Any nonhuman species with a leftward heart or humans without the claimed typical displacement refutes uniqueness; side temperature can test the proposed reason separately.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: comparative whole-body anatomy for organ position

candidate_datasets.name: The Cancer Imaging Archive
candidate_datasets.role: public human thoracic imaging suitable for heart-position measurements

obstacles: Cardiac apex direction and organ centroid are different measures.
Soft-tissue whole-body scans are sparse across species.
The coldness explanation lacks matched side-temperature data.
rationale: Position is directly measurable and public imaging can test humans and selected animals. Comparative coverage and the proposed thermal mechanism remain inadequate for the full universal claim.

operationalization: Use CT, histology, and veterinary anatomy to record ossa cordis in horses, cattle breeds, and other mammals. A normal ossified cardiac skeleton in another animal, or absence in the named taxa, refutes the exclusivity.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT data potentially showing mineralized cardiac skeletons in mammal specimens

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: comparative mammalian anatomy accounts

obstacles: Small cardiac bones may be absent from skeletal preparations and missed without soft-tissue CT.
Occurrence varies with age, breed, and calcification criteria.
A certain kind of ox is unspecified.
rationale: Cardiac ossification is a direct anatomical trait, and existing veterinary evidence can test several taxa. Public specimen coverage is not broad or standardized enough to establish uniqueness across mammals.

operationalization: Count anatomically defined heart chambers across blooded animals and model chamber number as a function of adult body size and lineage. Small animals with more chambers or large animals with fewer directly refute the asserted size rule.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: comparative vertebrate circulatory anatomy and body size

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: cardiac and whole-body anatomical imaging where available

obstacles: Atrium, ventricle, sinus venosus, and partial septa make chamber counting scheme-dependent.
Phylogeny strongly confounds size.
Soft-tissue cardiac data are not comprehensive.
rationale: Modern comparative anatomy provides many decisive size and chamber examples. The universal scope and chamber-definition differences require harmonization, but a substantial portion is resolvable.

operationalization: Define relative heart mass and standardized threat-boldness behavior, then test their association across the named mammals and a broader phylogenetic sample. A null or positive association between relative heart size and courage refutes the direction.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: body size and qualitative behavior accounts for the named mammals

obstacles: Timid and courageous are not standardized across species.
Heart mass and behavioral assays are rarely available for the same individuals or taxa.
Body size, metabolism, and domestication are strong confounds.
rationale: The relationship is testable in principle, but current public data do not jointly measure comparable boldness and heart size across the required species. Qualitative natural-history labels cannot adequately discriminate the proposed relation.

operationalization: Use lineage tracing and isotopic nutrient-flow data to quantify the contribution of blood-borne cells and molecules to each tissue during development and maintenance. Tissues built from local progenitors while merely receiving nutrients would refute a literal blood-as-material reading.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus
candidate_datasets.role: public lineage, developmental, and tissue-formation experiments

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: public developmental lineage and vascular imaging

obstacles: Material could mean cellular precursor, nutrient source, or transport medium.
No dataset traces every body part across all blooded animals.
Vessel distribution alone does not establish material origin.
rationale: Modern developmental data can distinguish blood cells from transported nutrients in model organisms. Ambiguous material language and universal scope permit only partial resolution.

operationalization: Across fishes and other vertebrates, code lungs and gills and analyze respiratory heat exchange from measured water or air flow and body temperature. Lung-bearing fishes refute never, while oxygen uptake without meaningful cooling refutes the universal cooling function.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fish respiratory organs, habitats, and taxonomy

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: comparative respiratory physiology and anatomy accounts

obstacles: Some fishes possess lungs or use air breathing.
Respiration and thermoregulation are coupled differently in ectotherms and endotherms.
Gills exchange gases, ions, and heat simultaneously.
rationale: Organ presence is broadly documented and yields decisive counterexamples to the categorical fish statement. Existing data test the cooling mechanism only in selected taxa and do not establish cooling as the necessary primary function.

operationalization: Measure lung volume relative to body size, vascular fraction, tissue water content, compliance, and inflation capacity across mammals, birds, reptiles, and other oviparous vertebrates. Overlap or reversed group differences refute the categorical contrast.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: comparative respiratory anatomy and whole-body imaging

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode and respiratory anatomy accounts

obstacles: Bird lungs and air sacs complicate what counts as lung size and expansion.
Viviparity occurs in multiple vertebrate lineages.
Comparable vascular and compliance data are scattered.
rationale: The anatomical and material properties are measurable, but no unified public dataset contains them across the stated reproductive groups. Existing evidence can test representative clades and individual components.

operationalization: Code homologues of heart and liver and all other defined viscera across vertebrate lineages. A blooded animal lacking either organ or another viscus present in every sampled lineage refutes the corresponding universal or uniqueness statement.

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: cross-species organ definitions, homologies, and taxonomic constraints

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: comparative vertebrate internal anatomy

obstacles: Liver-like organs and hearts differ in organization among basal vertebrates.
Only these depends on a fixed list and definition of viscera.
Universal absence is difficult to establish from incomplete coding.
rationale: Comparative anatomy and ontologies can test major vertebrate groups with clear counterexamples. Exhaustive coverage and the category of viscera limit full resolution.

operationalization: Code urinary bladder presence across birds, reptiles, and fishes, with tortoises and turtles separated, using a fixed definition that excludes transient cloacal expansion. Any nontortoise covered species with a true bladder refutes the claimed exception pattern.

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: cross-species urinary anatomy and taxonomic constraints

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: comparative excretory anatomy of birds, reptiles, and fishes

obstacles: Urinary bladder and cloacal urine storage may be confused.
Fish urinary anatomy is highly diverse.
Organ-presence data are not exhaustively coded at species level.
rationale: Bladder presence is a standard anatomical character and resources cover major lineages. The universal wording and organ-definition edge cases make the available test partial rather than exhaustive.

operationalization: Inspect renal anatomy across birds, fishes, reptiles, and tortoises, distinguishing true kidneys from kidney-like bodies by histology and excretory function. A true kidney in any non-tortoise feathered or scaled animal refutes the categorical claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: cross-species kidney anatomy and homology

candidate_datasets.name: Bgee
candidate_datasets.role: cross-species expression data indexed to kidneys and renal structures

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: comparative vertebrate excretory anatomy

obstacles: Aristotle's kidney category may exclude flattened avian kidneys by definition.
Species-level completeness is lower than class-level anatomy.
rationale: Renal organs are well-defined and extensively represented in public anatomical and expression resources across the target classes. Existing data can decisively resolve the core absence and tortoise-only exception claim.

operationalization: Measure the cranial-caudal position of paired kidneys in standardized body coordinates across species. Any typical species or individual with the left kidney higher than or level with the right refutes always.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: comparative whole-body soft-tissue imaging where kidneys are visible

candidate_datasets.name: The Cancer Imaging Archive
candidate_datasets.role: public human abdominal imaging for kidney-position distributions

obstacles: Soft-tissue imaging coverage outside humans and models is limited.
Body axis and higher must be defined for nonupright animals.
Developmental anomalies should be distinguished from typical anatomy.
rationale: Position has an obvious quantitative criterion and public scans can test humans and selected animals. Existing comparative coverage does not match all kidney-bearing animals, so the universal remains only partially resolvable.

operationalization: Define laughter acoustically and behaviorally in advance, and define tickling as a response to light tactile stimulation; then search experimental recordings across primates and other mammals. A nonhuman animal meeting either definition refutes uniqueness.

candidate_datasets.name: Macaulay Library
candidate_datasets.role: public animal audio and video that can document laughter-like vocal behavior

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: public behavioral datasets, including comparative vocalization studies

obstacles: Laughter may be defined narrowly as human laughter or broadly by homology and function.
Ticklishness requires controlled stimulation and is sparsely sampled.
Absence in untested species cannot establish human uniqueness.
rationale: Existing recordings and experiments can decisively test selected nonhuman counterexamples. Definition sensitivity and sparse systematic sampling prevent full resolution of uniqueness across animals.

operationalization: Code upper and lower incisor presence and count distinct stomach chambers in viviparous blooded animals, beginning with the named taxa. Any qualifying animal with multiple true stomach chambers refutes the universal.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: mammalian dentition and digestive anatomy accounts

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: comparative skull and digestive anatomy where soft tissue is available

obstacles: Foregut compartments may be called chambers of one stomach or separate stomachs.
Viviparous nonmammalian vertebrates broaden the literal scope.
Organ coding is incomplete beyond common mammals.
rationale: Dentition and stomach organization are standard traits and the named mammals are well documented. Definitions and incomplete broad coverage prevent an exhaustive test of all qualifying animals.

operationalization: Across the named ruminants and camel, code horn state, upper incisors, chewing behavior, and foregut chambers. Exceptions to the trait package refute the anatomy; causal compensation requires showing chamber complexity changes digestive performance specifically because incisors are absent.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: ruminant dentition, digestion, and life-history accounts

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: skull and digestive-system anatomy for ungulates

obstacles: Camels are multichambered but hornless.
Trait co-occurrence does not establish compensatory causation.
Stomach chamber definitions vary.
rationale: Existing comparative anatomy readily tests the co-occurring traits and named examples. It has weaker discriminating power for the asserted reason, which is confounded by diet and shared ancestry.

operationalization: Define rumination as regurgitation and remastication of previously swallowed food, observe Mediterranean Sparisoma cretense, and search standardized feeding observations across fishes. Another fish meeting the definition or failure by Scarus refutes uniqueness.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fish feeding ecology, behavior, and taxonomy

candidate_datasets.name: Macaulay Library
candidate_datasets.role: public fish behavior videos potentially documenting feeding and regurgitation

obstacles: Apparent rumination may be pharyngeal processing rather than stomach regurgitation.
Negative behavior evidence is sparse across fish diversity.
Historical Scarus mapping is not completely certain.
rationale: The behavior can be operationalized and selected observations may test the named fish. Existing public resources do not systematically record regurgitation and remastication across fishes, so the sole-species claim cannot be fully resolved.
